## Tool call descriptions

Whenever you call a tool that asks for user approval (Bash especially), populate the
call's `description` with a **plain-English explanation of what you are doing and
why**, not a restatement of the command. Instead of "Run kubectl delete pods --all -n
prod", write "Delete the orphaned canary pods from yesterday's failed rollout so the
next deploy starts clean". For Bash and shell pipelines the description is often the
only thing the user sees before approving; for Edit/Write the diff is visible, so
descriptions can be terser. This applies to subagents too, since their tool calls
surface to the same user.

## Response style

Applies to every piece of English you produce, whatever its size or destination:
chat replies, reports, plans, reviews, code comments and docstrings, commit
messages, PR and issue bodies, error strings, and CLI help text.

**Read `.axis/context/refs/prose-style.md` before you write.** It carries every rule
with an example and a fix for each, and reading it is a required step in any task
that produces English. The rules bind a one-line code comment the same as a
twenty-page plan. If the file is missing, run `axis sync`.

The reference covers what goes into a piece of writing: lead with the outcome, stay
short by choosing what to include, match the altitude to the question, never trade
correctness for brevity, and state only what is. It then covers how the sentences
read: flat and declarative, one idea each, free of the nine rhetorical tics and the
five surface tells it names.

## Commit conventions

When you make a git commit, **do not attribute it to yourself.** No
`Co-Authored-By:` trailer, no "authored/generated by AI" line, no agent or model
name in the message. Commits are authored by the human running the session, so write
the message in their voice: what the change does and why, nothing more.

The subject line is `type(scope): summary`, at most 72 characters, with the type in
lowercase from this list: feat, fix, refactor, docs, test, chore, build, ci, perf,
revert. The scope is the workspace or area the change touches, such as `cli`,
`catalog`, `policy`, `site`, or `infra`.

**The summary is one imperative clause that starts with a verb.** It has to complete
the sentence "If applied, this commit will ___": `add the pipelines table` completes
it, `the four checks, and one shape for a failed load` does not. The tics banned in
Response style bind the subject line too, and a subject welding two things with
`, and` is two commits.

The body says why the change was made; the diff already shows what.

**One commit carries one revertable change, so slice a large working tree without
being asked.** A session that leaves 200 files across several topics is a sequence
of commits: stage each slice with a path-scoped `git add` or `git add -p`, and order
them so each stands on its own, with a contract ahead of the code that binds it.
Slice by what changed, not by directory or file type. When a change genuinely cannot
be separated, say so and write one subject that is true of all of it.

A release commit is the one exception and reads `release vX.Y.Z`.

## Agents

This repository uses **AXIS standard SDLC agents** — focused workflows with explicit
scope, referenced by name. Each one's full operating procedure lives in its own skill file,
which your tool discovers automatically:

- **GitHub Copilot:** `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (self-contained),
  plus each tool's own agent directory for isolated subagents.

Run one by name, or list the skills directory to see the installed roster.

A repo-local agent is registered with `axis config agent add <name>`; its body is
the team's own prose at `.axis/custom-agents/<name>.md`, authored by following
`.axis/context/refs/fill-agent.md`, and `axis sync` projects it onto every surface
above.

## Playbooks

Best-practice references for this repo's stack are materialized under
`.axis/playbooks/` (one `<domain>-<name>.md` per area). When a task touches one
of these areas, read the matching playbook first and check your work against its
Checklist before reporting done.

**If `.axis/playbooks/` or `.axis/context/refs/` is missing, say so and run
`axis sync` before continuing.** Both are gitignored, so a fresh clone does not
carry them, and a task without them silently loses its playbooks and the
prose-style reference rather than failing. The sync is idempotent and writes only
axis-owned files. https://axis.egen.dev covers installing the binary.
